title: The Holocaust
summary: The Holocaust was the systematic, state-sponsored genocide perpetrated by Nazi Germany and its collaborators between 1941 and 1945, murdering approximately six million European Jews alongside hundreds of thousands of Romani people, disabled persons, and other targeted groups across occupied Europe.
card: Following years of anti-Jewish persecution and forced emigration from 1933, Nazi Germany initiated systematic mass murder following the June 1941 invasion of the Soviet Union. Mobile killing squads shot roughly two million people in eastern Europe, while the January 1942 Wannsee Conference coordinated continental deportations to industrial killing centres including Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, and Bełżec. Approximately six million Jews—two-thirds of European Jewry—were murdered before Allied liberation in 1945.
what:
The Holocaust was the state-sponsored annihilation of European Jewry by National Socialist Germany and its collaborators. Ideologically grounded in Adolf Hitler's racial antisemitism, the regime began systematic persecution upon seizing power in 1933, stripping German Jews of citizenship through the 1935 Nuremberg Laws and dispossessing communal property. The policy escalated into total continental genocide following the invasion of the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941.

Mass murder proceeded across two principal operational mechanisms. In the occupied Soviet territories, SS Einsatzgruppen, Order Police battalions, and local auxiliary collaborators carried out mobile shooting operations, slaughtering approximately two million Jews and dumping their bodies into mass graves, as at Babi Yar and Ponary. Concurrently, the regime constructed specialized killing centres equipped with carbon monoxide and Zyklon B gas chambers across occupied Poland. On 20 January 1942, SS-Obergruppenführer Reinhard Heydrich convened the Wannsee Conference in Berlin, securing inter-agency bureaucratic coordination to deport over eleven million targeted European Jews. Under Adolf Eichmann's logistical management, railways transported families from across Europe to extermination camps at Chełmno, Bełżec, Sobibór, Treblinka, and Auschwitz-Birkenau.

Victims faced dehumanization and death. Survivor Primo Levi recorded that arrival at the camps stripped prisoners of clothing, hair, and names, imposing "the demolition of a man." Eyewitness Hermann Friedrich Graebe described families calmly undressing before being shot atop layers of corpses in mass pits at Dubno, testimony submitted to the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg. In total, approximately six million Jews perished—representing two-thirds of European Jewish life—alongside at least 250,000 Romani people in the Porajmos, up to 300,000 disabled individuals murdered in institutional euthanasia programs, and over three million Soviet prisoners of war.

Historians debate whether this genocide unfolded from a long-held intentional blueprint or developed through bureaucratic improvisation and cumulative radicalization as wartime deportation schemes collapsed. Camp classifications also reflect evolving research; while earlier scholarship designated Majdanek as a sixth primary extermination facility, current historians classify it primarily as a concentration and forced-labor camp where mass gassings and shooting operations occurred intermittently.

uncertainty.note: Mass murder operations commenced with the invasion of the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941 and ended with Germany's unconditional surrender on 8 May 1945; state-sponsored persecution, legal disenfranchisement, and forced emigration preceded this phase from January 1933.

how:
The genocide developed through distinct, escalating phases orchestrated by Nazi state leadership:
1. Ideological and Legal Disenfranchisement (1933–1939): State-sanctioned antisemitism institutionalized legal discrimination, the Nuremberg Laws of 1935, economic dispossession, and organized terror during the Kristallnacht pogroms of November 1938, driving coerced emigration.
2. Territorial Concentration and Ghettoization (1939–1941): Following the invasion of Poland in September 1939, German authorities concentrated millions of Polish Jews into enclosed, overcrowded urban ghettos—such as Warsaw and Łódź—where starvation, forced labor, and deliberate denial of sanitation caused hundreds of thousands of deaths.
3. Mobile Mass Shootings (June 1941–1943): The invasion of the Soviet Union marked the transition to physical annihilation. Four mobile SS Einsatzgruppen (A, B, C, D) followed the Wehrmacht advance, supported by police units and local auxiliaries, executing over 1.5 to 2 million Jews in mass open-air shootings across Ukraine, Belarus, and the Baltic States.
4. Industrialized Gassing and Operation Reinhard (1941–1944): In autumn 1941, the regime developed stationary gas facilities. Chełmno commenced operations with gas vans in December 1941. Following the January 1942 Wannsee Conference, Operation Reinhard established dedicated extermination camps at Bełżec, Sobibór, and Treblinka using carbon monoxide engine exhaust. At Auschwitz-Birkenau, large-scale selections sent over one million victims directly to industrial Zyklon B gas chambers and crematoria.
5. Death Marches and Collapse (1944–1945): As Soviet armies advanced, the SS dismantled camp installations to destroy evidence, forcing surviving starving prisoners westward on brutal winter death marches until final liberation by Allied forces.
why_it_matters:
The Holocaust decimated European Jewry, extinguishing centuries-old religious, literary, and social communities across Central and Eastern Europe. Demographically, two out of every three European Jews were murdered, destroying the vibrant Yiddish-speaking civilization of the Pale of Settlement and creating millions of displaced persons whose plight accelerated the political drive to establish the State of Israel in 1948.

In jurisprudence and ethics, Nazi atrocities compelled the international community to forge entirely new legal doctrines. Raphael Lemkin coined the concept of genocide in response to these crimes, leading directly to the United Nations Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in 1948. At Nuremberg, the International Military Tribunal established the permanent principle that sovereign heads of state and military commanders bear individual criminal liability for crimes against humanity and war crimes, rejecting the defense of superior orders and laying the foundation for modern international criminal courts.

The event permanently reshaped global moral consciousness regarding totalitarian power, institutional complicity, and the catastrophic dangers of state-engineered racism. Had Nazi Germany triumphed or concluded a negotiated peace in the East, the regime would have completed the extermination of all eleven million targeted European Jews listed at Wannsee, establishing a continental slave empire anchored in racial purity. Without the documentation preserved by survivors and recovered by archives like Arolsen and Yad Vashem, historical denial might have obscured the mechanics of industrialized state murder, weakening contemporary legal and educational barriers against future genocide.

related.because: Adolf Hitler's racial antisemitic ideology and supreme political authority authorized the physical annihilation of European Jewry.
The catastrophic scale of Nazi genocide spurred the United Nations to establish international legal frameworks protecting fundamental human rights.
Wartime atrocities and the mass murder of civilians prompted the comprehensive revision of humanitarian law in the Fourth Geneva Convention.

perspectives.holder: Intentionalist historians (e.g. Lucy Dawidowicz, Gerald Fleming)
perspectives.account: Argue that Adolf Hitler harbored a long-standing, premeditated blueprint for the physical annihilation of European Jewry dating from the 1920s, which was methodically executed as military conditions permitted.

perspectives.holder: Functionalist and structuralist historians (e.g. Martin Broszat, Hans Mommsen)
perspectives.account: Argue that the genocide arose through cumulative radicalization and improvisational administrative competition within the polycratic Nazi state, escalating into total physical extermination only when wartime territorial schemes collapsed in late 1941.

audience_note: Contains historical documentation of state-sponsored mass genocide, industrial extermination camps, gas chambers, mobile mass execution pits, extreme torture, and medical experiments perpetrated by the Nazi regime.

importance.justification: The Holocaust was the state-sponsored industrial genocide of six million European Jews and millions of other victims, permanently transforming international human rights law, genocide conventions, and moral philosophy.

reviewer_note: The exact proportion of victims killed by mobile shooting operations versus camp gas chambers remains subject to ongoing archival research in post-Soviet local mass graves.
parent_reconciliation: This record documents the Holocaust as the genocide of six million European Jews alongside Romani and disabled victims; these figures reconcile with the civilian genocide totals in parent record 1939-world-war-ii.
